title: Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions
authors: Mohammed Barhoush, Tomoyuki Morimae, Ramis Movassagh
abstract: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qIO) aims to make a quantum circuit unintelligible while preserving its functionality. It serves as a foundational primitive for advanced applications, such as witness encryption (WE) for QMA, non-interactive zero-knowledge arguments for QMA, and attribute-based encryption for BQP. Despite its importance, constructing qIO from standard assumptions remains a major open problem.   In this work, we prove that the security of WE for QMA cannot be based on any falsifiable cryptographic assumption via a restricted class of quantum black-box reductions. Because qIO for null quantum circuits implies WE for QMA, this also separates null-qIO from falsifiable assumptions. Since almost all standard cryptographic assumptions are falsifiable, our result presents a barrier to basing qIO on standard cryptographic assumptions.   The reductions we rule out are restricted: the reduction must query the adversary classically, non-adaptively, at the same security parameter, and only on honestly generated ciphertexts. Moreover, our impossibility applies only to WE with classical ciphertexts, and therefore does not rule out qIO with obfuscators whose output is a quantum state. Ruling out more general reductions, as well as more general forms of WE and qIO, remains open.   Our impossibility relies on the existence of a QMA-QCIP[2] gap problem, an average-case assumption postulating a QMA language that cannot be verified with two messages of classical communication.
summary: This paper tackles the fundamental cryptographic question of whether quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qIO) can be secured using standard, falsifiable computational assumptions. By proving an impossibility result under specific reduction constraints, the authors show that qIO security for QMA cannot be based on these assumptions. This establishes a significant theoretical barrier for constructing such primitives.
main_problem: The paper aims to separate the security of Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation (qIO) and Witness Encryption (WE) for QMA from standard, falsifiable cryptographic assumptions.
main_result: It proves that the security of WE for QMA cannot be based on any falsifiable cryptographic assumption under a restricted class of quantum black-box reductions, thereby establishing a structural barrier for qIO security.
method: The proof utilizes a restricted class of quantum black-box reductions and relies on the existence of a QMA–QCIP[2] gap problem as a necessary assumption.
model_or_system: The work operates within the framework of quantum computation, focusing on quantum circuits, the complexity class QMA, and cryptographic primitives like qIO and WE.
key_observables: The advantage of the qIO-adversary, which measures the success probability of breaking the obfuscation scheme.
important_parameters: The security parameter $n$, and the assumption of a QMA–QCIP[2] gap problem.
main_assumptions: The result is restricted to WE with classical ciphertexts and relies on the existence of the QMA–QCIP[2] gap problem; it does not cover all possible reductions or quantum state outputs.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the formal definitions for null-qIO and WE for QMA, then constructs the restricted null-qIO reduction, culminating in a theorem that proves the separation between the security of qIO and falsifiable assumptions.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, the concepts of quantum obfuscation and complexity separation are foundational to understanding the limits of quantum cryptography, which underpins many advanced quantum information protocols.
